profile.summary: Migrate approximately 150,000 accounts and contacts from Salesforce to Kestrel within three weeks, supporting Vietnamese and Japanese names from regional sales offices.
Implement Azure AD single sign-on and provisioning for 4,000 staff to meet an audit requirement within two weeks.
Investigate and resolve performance issues with the portfolio dashboard causing slow load times during quarter-end.
Launch Fund IV by having 5,000 limited partners e-sign subscription documents in Kestrel within 15 working days.
Implement automated daily synchronization of user accounts from Workday for new hires and terminations.
Translate the public marketing website into French and German before the trade show next month.

briefing.headline: Kaito Freight needs 150,000 accounts and contacts migrated from Salesforce in 15 days with Vietnamese and Japanese names. Similar past migrations suffered from encoding failures, data residency oversights, and delayed dedupe agreements.

howItWent.text: KST-104 took 18 days instead of 10 because dedupe rules and picklist mappings were agreed late, and required two dry runs.
KST-162 finished a day early by reusing the KST-104 mapper and getting dedupe rules and picklists signed on day 2.
KST-147 escalated due to data residency issues and broken Vietnamese and Japanese characters caused by non-UTF-8 exports.

differences.note: 3.9x the volume of KST-104. Expect dry runs, exports and checks to take longer.
Less time than KST-104 really took. Cut scope, add people, or reset expectations now.
Non-English data that KST-104 did not have. KST-147 was escalated over broken characters: force UTF-8 and check samples with a native speaker.
Different region. Confirm data residency and which tenant/region to use at kickoff.
Only the notes are left from Minh Tran. Tom Becker also worked on it: ask them.
KST-104 did not go to plan. Read its lessons before estimating.

differences.before: Standard response times on emails and review cycles
differences.now: Regional sales offices in Hanoi and Tokyo requiring direct engagement across time zones
differences.note: Time zone differences and multi-office sign-offs may slow down review cycles during a tight 15-day window.

plan.text: Confirm data residency requirements and tenant region with Kaito Freight at kickoff.
Send the Migration dedupe checklist v2 and picklist mapping sheet to the client on day 1 for written sign-off.
Enforce UTF-8 CSV exports from Salesforce and run encoding-check.py before any data load.
Execute two dry runs using sf-export-mapper.py adapted for the 150k volume.
Have native speakers in Hanoi and Tokyo check a sample of 200 Vietnamese and Japanese records each before go-live.

reuse.why: Transforms Salesforce Data Loader CSVs into Kestrel import format using picklist mappings.
Covers fund-entity and regional ownership questions for deduplication.
Detects mojibake and encoding issues in CSV files before loading non-English text.
Identifies the correct region and tenant configuration for APAC clients.

lessons.text: Force UTF-8 exports and run encoding-check.py before ANY load with non-English data.
Have a native speaker check a sample of each language before go-live, not after.
Check data residency at kickoff. Moving to another region later costs 3 days.
Agree the dedupe rule in writing before the first dry run and send the picklist mapping sheet on day 1.
Plan for two dry runs, noting that higher record volumes will increase export and check times.

openQuestions: Which specific regional data residency tenant should be used for Kaito Freight?
Who are the designated native speakers in the Hanoi and Tokyo offices who can validate the 200-sample checks?
Can the client commit to a 24-hour turnaround on the dedupe checklist and picklist mapping sheet given the compressed 3-week timeline?

briefing.headline: Strong precedent in KST-128 (Azure AD SSO and SCIM), which ran 9 days late due to missing IT admin consent and bug ENG-882, but KST-178 proved upfront checklists cut delivery time.

howItWent.text: KST-128 was delayed by a week because the initial client contact was in HR and could not grant Global Admin consent in Azure AD.
KST-128 hit a known bug (ENG-882) where SCIM deactivation left users in group memberships, which was resolved by upgrading the tenant to release 4.12.
KST-178 showed that running an SSO/SCIM kickoff checklist up front reduced delivery time to 4 days.

differences.note: 1.6x the volume of KST-128. Expect dry runs, exports and checks to take longer.
Less time than KST-128 really took. Cut scope, add people, or reset expectations now.
Only the notes are left from Sofia Reyes. Daniel Okafor also worked on it: ask them.
KST-128 did not go to plan. Read its lessons before estimating.
Tight turnaround for higher user volume and audit requirement.

plan.text: Verify the client's IT admin who can grant Azure AD Global Admin consent is named and on the kickoff call.
Ensure the client tenant is on release 4.12 or later to avoid bug ENG-882 regarding SCIM group memberships.
Configure Azure AD enterprise app, attribute mapping, and ensure JIT is off and emails are lower-cased.
Establish a break-glass admin account outside of SSO.
Run dry runs and exports early to account for the 4,000 user volume.
Conduct a witnessed leaver test with the client's IT security team.

reuse.why: Provides step-by-step Azure AD enterprise app setup, attribute mapping, and the leaver test script.
Contains pre-flight items including IT admin contact, release version, JIT off, and email normalisation.
Covers common SAML errors like clock skew and NameID format.

lessons.text: Get the client's IT admin (the person who can grant consent) named at kickoff. Business contacts cannot do it.
Test deprovisioning explicitly, including group memberships. Security teams will check this.
Always keep one break-glass admin outside SSO before enforcing it.
Running the SSO/SCIM kickoff checklist up front turned a longer project into 4 days.

openQuestions: Who is the designated client IT administrator with Global Admin rights in Azure AD?
Is the client's Azure/Kestrel tenant already on release 4.12 or later?
Has a break-glass admin account been designated outside of SSO?

briefing.headline: Strong precedent from KST-125 and KST-185 (month-end/search slowness caused by competing batch jobs). KST-125 took 9 days instead of 3 due to estimation issues.

howItWent.text: KST-125 was escalated due to month-end slowness taking 30+ seconds, missing the 3-day estimate by 6 days and finishing in 9 days.
Root cause in KST-125 was a custom filter field 'cost_center' lacking an index combined with a competing month-end batch import.
Resolution in KST-125 involved adding an index on the custom field and shifting the batch import out of business hours.

differences.note: KST-125 did not go to plan. Read its lessons before estimating.
Quarter-end volumes or concurrent reporting might be higher than month-end.

plan.text: Use the Performance triage checklist to ask the client WHEN the dashboard is slow and identify exact peak hours.
Check dashboard filters for unindexed custom fields (e.g., cost_center style fields).
Investigate competing quarter-end batch imports or data loads running during business hours.
Add necessary database indexes and coordinate with the client to reschedule overlapping batch jobs.
Send daily status updates to the client's finance team throughout the investigation.

lessons.text: Ask WHEN it is slow, not just what. Quarter-end or month-end slowness usually points to a competing batch job.
Check filters on custom fields first because they are not indexed by default.
In an escalation, send a daily status update even when there is no news; clients care deeply about communication.

openQuestions: Exact time window when the portfolio dashboard becomes slow during quarter-end?
Are there any batch jobs, imports, or syncs scheduled to run at the same time as quarter-end reporting?
Which specific filters or custom fields are applied on the portfolio dashboard?

briefing.headline: The closest precedent is KST-131 (Sable Ventures), which finished 5 days late due to late PDF changes. The main difference now is that 5,000 limited partners need to be onboarded in 15 working days while legal is still editing the agreement.

howItWent.text: KST-131 took 13 days instead of 8 because late edits to the subscription agreement shifted every page after page 12 and broke all 41 tagged fields.
KST-187 took 14 days instead of 8 because bulk invitation emails landed in spam until a custom sending domain (SPF/DKIM) was configured.
KST-160 completed on time in 5 days by agreeing on a roles matrix and batching invites.

differences.note: 1.7x the volume of KST-131. Expect dry runs, exports and checks to take longer.
Only the notes are left from Marco Bianchi. An Nguyen also worked on it: ask them.
KST-131 did not go to plan. Read its lessons before estimating.

differences.before: Agreements were finalized prior to tagging in past cases
differences.now: Legal is still editing the agreement while deadline is in 15 days
differences.note: Risk of retagging rework if tagging starts before a written document freeze.

plan.text: Ask An Nguyen for context on KST-131 and KST-187 as Marco Bianchi left the company.
Obtain written confirmation from legal to freeze the document version before tagging fields in Kestrel.
Set up the client's custom sending domain with SPF/DKIM before sending any bulk invites.
Tag signature, date, and initial fields on the frozen subscription agreement PDF.
Test the tagged document with 5 internal signers before launching the bulk campaign.
Send bulk invites for the 5,000 limited partners in batches of 500 to keep bounce handling manageable.
Check open rates after 48 hours to monitor deliverability.

reuse.why: Contains document freeze, field tagging, and signer test steps for e-sign campaigns.
Provides instructions on setting up custom sending domains with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC to avoid spam filters.
Spreadsheet to align on roles and permissions before starting onboarding.

lessons.text: Freeze the document version in writing before tagging fields. Any late page change breaks every tag after it.
Test with a few internal signers before a bulk invite.
Send bulk invites in batches of 500 to keep bounce handling manageable.
For any bulk email to investors, set up the client's custom sending domain (SPF/DKIM) BEFORE the first invite.
Check open rates after 48 hours, not after a week.

openQuestions: When exactly will legal provide the final, unedited version of the subscription agreement in writing?
Does the client have a custom sending domain ready for SPF/DKIM configuration, or do we need IT assistance?
Can An Nguyen support this launch given that Marco Bianchi left the company?

briefing.headline: The team has not done Workday integration before (closest precedent KST-170/KST-128); past provisioning projects ran late due to unmanaged IT contacts and duplicate user edge cases.

howItWent.text: KST-170 finished 5 days late because JIT provisioning was left on, creating ~140 duplicate users when email casing differed.
KST-128 finished 9 days late because the initial contact was in HR rather than IT, delaying admin consent by a week.
KST-178 finished on time in 4 days by applying a kickoff checklist addressing JIT, email normalisation, and IT admin involvement upfront.

differences.note: The team has never worked with Workday before. No playbook exists, verify API access and limits in week 1.
KST-170 did not go to plan. Read its lessons before estimating.
Workday API structure and limits are unverified by the team; no playbook exists.

plan.text: Identify and name the client's IT administrator who can grant Workday integration and API access at kickoff.
Verify Workday API access, permissions, and rate limits in week 1 since no playbook exists.
Ensure existing user emails are normalised to lower case before enabling automated synchronization to prevent duplicates.
Map Workday employee attributes (such as department and termination status) to Kestrel teams and access states.
Run a live deprovisioning and new hire test with the client's IT security or auditor present.

lessons.text: Get the client's IT admin (the person who can grant system consent/API access) named at kickoff; business contacts cannot do it.
lessons.from: Sofia Reyes (Integration Engineer, LEFT THE COMPANY)

lessons.text: Normalise existing users' emails to lower case first to prevent duplicate account creation.
Test deprovisioning explicitly, including group memberships, with IT security or auditors watching.
Running the kickoff checklist up front turns a multi-week provisioning project into a streamlined execution.

openQuestions: Who is the specific IT administrator with permissions to configure Workday integration and API access?
What specific Workday endpoints, reports, or webhooks will be used for night-time synchronization of new hires and terminations?
Do existing user emails in Kestrel match the email format stored in Workday to prevent duplicate account creation?

briefing.headline: The team has not done website translation before; KST-181 serves as the closest operational precedent regarding strict deadlines and multi-language/localization tasks.

howItWent.text: KST-181 suffered a two-week delay waiting for a DPA signature from the client's legal team before any data could be touched.
KST-181 completed the core technical work successfully once the script and encoding checks were established.

differences.before: Data migration and backend system configuration
differences.now: Public marketing website translation into French and German
differences.note: Team has no internal precedent or artifacts for website translation or linguistic localization.

plan.text: Clarify exact deadline date and list of pages/assets on the public marketing website needing translation.
Establish ownership and confirm availability for the 20-day timeframe.
Inventory all text content, UI strings, and marketing assets required for French and German localization.
Execute translation and localization workflow for both languages.

lessons.text: For tight deadline projects, identify and clear any administrative or legal blockers immediately.

openQuestions: Do you have existing translation memories, glossaries, or preferred translation tools we should use?
Are the marketing website texts already exported in a format (like XLIFF, JSON, or CSV), or do we need to extract them from the CMS?
Who from your team will review and sign off on the French and German translations before the trade show?
